sections.title: What does a crossing tell us?
sections.label: Locate a root
sections.intro: The height of the graph is the value of the function. For a given input the graph can be above, below or on the horizontal axis. A root is the input that gives height zero. The graph at the left test point and the right test point can show where to look.

blocks.html: If a function is continuous on the closed interval and its endpoint values have opposite signs, there is at least one zero inside. In symbols, \(f(a)f(b)<0\) gives a root in \(a

blocks.html: An endpoint with a negative function value can have a positive input. The test concerns the heights.

sections.title: How do I turn an intersection into a root?
sections.label: Subtract one side
sections.intro: At an intersection both curves have the same height at the same horizontal input. This can be tested without drawing either curve accurately. Subtract one height from the other to make a new function.

blocks.html: For \(L(x)=R(x)\), define \(f(x)=L(x)-R(x)\). When its sign switches, the curve that was higher at the first input is lower at the second. Any zero of the difference is an intersection of the original graphs wherever both sides are defined.
The individual signs of the two heights can agree at both test points. It is the order of the heights that can reverse.
Use the same subtraction order throughout. Either difference works when used consistently.

sections.title: Which adjacent inputs should I choose?
sections.label: Scan ordered test values
sections.intro: When no bracket is supplied, a sketch, table or a few carefully chosen calculator evaluations can provide one. Start with the part of the domain proposed in the question. Then arrange the test inputs from least to greatest and track the sign column.

blocks.html: Two adjacent inputs with different signs are enough to locate a continuous crossing. A smaller interval makes the initial estimate more informative. The table shows an interval and therefore a range of possible values for the unknown.
Checking only the first and last values may hide a shorter bracket or a second crossing.
If asked for consecutive integers, carry out the sign test at two consecutive integer inputs. Give those actual inputs.

sections.title: What if an endpoint already solves it?
sections.label: Handle a value of zero
sections.intro: When substitution gives an exact zero, the corresponding input is a root. Opposite signs are a sufficient way to locate a root when the endpoints are both nonzero. An exact endpoint instead gives its value directly.

blocks.html: Treat an endpoint root separately. When the question asks for another root strictly inside, find another bracket or use additional information about the shape of the function.
A value displayed as zero after rounding can still be positive or negative.
If the arithmetic permits, use an exact expression at a suspect endpoint before deciding it is zero.

sections.title: When can I say that the root is unique?
sections.label: Add a reason for uniqueness
sections.intro: Continuity gives existence when the endpoints have opposite signs. A strictly increasing or strictly decreasing function can cross the axis at most once in an interval. Use both statements when a question asks for the number of roots.

blocks.html: If you can show \(f'(x)>0\) at every interior point of the bracket, its graph is strictly increasing across that bracket. Other information such as a known graph shape or an exact factorisation can also prove that there is at most one root.
A single sign change across a broad interval can hide several crossings.
Separate the existence argument from the uniqueness argument. State the interval on which each applies.

glossary.definition: An input where the function value is zero.
Two test inputs enclosing a root.
A function has no gap or jump on the interval being used.
A point with the same input and output on both graphs.
A function that strictly increases or strictly decreases throughout an interval.

revision.body:
For an equation with two sides, test the difference. When a continuous function has opposite signs at the endpoints, a zero lies strictly between them.

Here \(f(1)=-7\) and \(f(2)=1\). The signs identify an interval containing the crossing.

FindingWhat to conclude
An exact zero at a test inputThat input is a root.
Opposite signs on a continuous intervalAt least one root.
Opposite signs and strict monotonicityExactly one root on that interval.

orig_9709_p3_num_sign_limits.description: Explain when signs miss a root or suggest a false bracket. Recognise touches, multiple crossings, asymptotes and cancelled holes.

sections.title: How can a graph meet the axis without crossing?
sections.label: Recognise a touching root
sections.intro: The sign test detects a switch between positive and negative values. For a square factor the graph may instead come down to zero and return to the same side. Inspect the shape of the graph or consider how many times the same factor occurs.

blocks.html: For \(f(x)=(x-a)^2\), the value at \(a\) is zero and all other values are positive. Two positive endpoint values are consistent with this root.

figure.alt: The square graph meets the axis at two without changing sign. The reciprocal graph changes sign across its vertical asymptote at two, where it is undefined.
figure.caption: At \(x=2\) the square reaches zero. The reciprocal has a gap in its domain and its values cannot be joined across the dashed line.

blocks.html: Equal signs do not justify the statement that there are no roots.
When factorisation exposes a repeated factor, check directly whether it vanishes in the interval.

blocks.title: Find the zero that a sign scan misses
blocks.prompt: For \(f(x)=(x+4)^2\) on \([-6,-2]\), give every root in the interval and choose the explanation that matches the graph.

options.option1: The graph crosses the axis twice

blocks.hint: Check the original domain before you interpret the endpoint signs.
blocks.solution:
\(f(-6)=4\) and \(f(-2)=4\).

The square is zero at \(x=-4\) and positive on both sides. The graph meets the axis at the vertex.

The root set is \(\{-4\}\).

sections.title: Can an asymptote look like a zero?
sections.label: Check continuity before signs
sections.intro: The curve drawn on one side of a vertical asymptote does not connect to the curve on the other. A change from negative to positive over the gap therefore does not prove that a value of zero is reached.

blocks.html: Before applying the sign test, inspect the whole bracket for a zero denominator, an invalid logarithm or another break. You may still test either side separately over an interval lying in the original domain.
An allowed left endpoint and an allowed right endpoint do not guarantee that every input between them is allowed.
State where the function is undefined when explaining why the test is inconclusive.

blocks.title: Reject a bracket crossing an asymptote
blocks.prompt: For \(f(x)=\frac{1}{x-5}\) on \([3,7]\), give every root in the interval and choose the explanation that matches the graph.

options.option1: The graph crosses the axis twice

blocks.hint: Check the original domain before you interpret the endpoint signs.
blocks.solution:
\(f(3)=-\frac{1}{2}\) and \(f(7)=\frac{1}{2}\).

At \(x=5\) the denominator is zero and the function is undefined. Its nonzero numerator cannot make the fraction equal to zero.

The root set is \(\varnothing\).

sections.title: Can the graph cross twice between tests?
sections.label: Read broad brackets carefully
sections.intro: If two simple roots lie between the test points, the sign can reverse at each root. Two reversals bring the value back to its starting sign. A sign table with a test point between the roots makes the two crossings visible.

blocks.html: In a continuous graph, equal signs provide no certificate for the number of roots. Look for turning points, split the interval, or use factorisation to count them. A sign change on a large bracket still guarantees existence but does not supply a count.
A smaller interval can help locate a single crossing. Its size alone does not prove uniqueness.
When a problem asks for all roots, make a separate case for each crossing or touching point.

blocks.title: Two positive trial values hide two roots
blocks.prompt: For \(f(x)=(x+1)(x-2)\) on \([-3,4]\), give every root in the interval and choose the explanation that matches the graph.

options.option1: The graph crosses the axis twice

blocks.hint: Check the original domain before you interpret the endpoint signs.
blocks.solution:
\(f(-3)=10\) and \(f(4)=10\).

Both factors give a root. Each simple root reverses the sign, so the graph finishes on the same side of the axis as it started.

The root set is \(\{-1,2\}\).

sections.title: Does cancellation fill in a missing input?
sections.label: Preserve the original domain
sections.intro: Cancelling a common factor is a valid simplification on the original domain of a fraction. An input that made the original denominator zero remains excluded. A simplified graph may look as though it contains a root where the original graph has a hole.

blocks.html: Record excluded values before simplifying. If the sole zero of the simplified expression is excluded, the original equation has no root there, even if function values on either side have opposite signs.
A graphing calculator can trace a simplified expression without displaying its missing point.
Check each candidate in the original expression after cancellation. Write an excluded input explicitly.

blocks.title: Check a cancelled candidate
blocks.prompt: For \(f(x)=\frac{(x-4)^2}{x-4}\) on \([2,6]\), give every root in the interval and choose the explanation that matches the graph.

options.option1: The graph crosses the axis twice

blocks.hint: Check the original domain before you interpret the endpoint signs.
blocks.solution:
\(f(2)=-2\) and \(f(6)=2\).

Cancellation gives \(x-4\) only when \(x\ne4\). The only candidate is excluded from the original domain, so the graph has a hole instead of a zero.

The root set is \(\varnothing\).

sections.title: What does multiplicity say about the sign?
sections.label: Distinguish crossings from touches
sections.intro: Near a root of a polynomial, the factors that do not vanish keep their sign. The vanishing factor controls what happens as the input moves through the root. An odd power changes sign and an even power keeps its sign.

blocks.html: A flat graph at a root can still cross the axis. For \(f(x)=(x-a)^3\), the function changes sign at \(a\) even though its gradient at that point is zero.
Do not classify a root by gradient zero alone. Compare the signs on both sides.
Use the factor and its multiplicity to support your description of the graph.

blocks.title: Distinguish a flat crossing from a touch
blocks.prompt: For \(f(x)=(x+3)^3\) on \([-5,-1]\), give every root in the interval and choose the explanation that matches the graph.

options.option1: The graph crosses the axis twice

The factor keeps the sign of its base because the power is odd. It is zero at \(x=-3\).

The root set is \(\{-3\}\).

solution: Both factors give a root. Each simple root reverses the sign, so the graph finishes on the same side of the axis as it started.

glossary.definition: A break in the function on the interval.
A vertical line approached by a branch whose magnitude becomes unbounded.
An input outside the original domain.
The power to which the root's linear factor occurs.
A root with the same sign on the two nearby sides.

revision.body:
Check continuity before interpreting \(f(a)f(b)<0\). For \(f(x)=\frac{(x-a)^2}{x-a}\), the simplification to \(x-a\) leaves \(x=a\) excluded.

PatternWhat to check
Same signsA touch or an even number of crossings may be hidden.
Different signsA zero is guaranteed if the function is continuous throughout.
After cancellationThe original excluded inputs still apply.
A horizontal tangentUse signs or multiplicity to distinguish touch from crossing.

  • Find any factor that vanishes in the bracket.
  • Use a graph or exact argument if endpoints alone are inconclusive.
revision.examTip: Describe whether there is an actual zero or a break in the domain before interpreting a change of sign.

orig_9709_p3_num_accuracy.description: Certify a numerical root to decimal places or significant figures. Find both rounding boundaries and check the original function on the correct branch.

sections.title: Which numbers round to the same answer?
sections.label: Find the rounding interval
sections.intro: A calculator approximation suggests which digits to write. To certify them, ask which nearby inputs would round to that same written value. The last digit determines the width of that window. For two decimal places, successive possible rounded values differ by \(0.01\).

blocks.html: For a candidate \(a\) correct to \(d\) decimal places, take half a unit in the last place. Test \(a-\frac12\times10^{-d}\) and \(a+\frac12\times10^{-d}\). A root strictly inside this interval rounds to \(a\).

figure.alt: The square-minus-6.5 curve is negative at 2.545 and positive at 2.555. Both test inputs surround the numbers that round to 2.55.
figure.caption: A root strictly between \(2.545\) and \(2.555\) rounds to \(2.55\) to two decimal places.

blocks.html: The test inputs for a two-decimal answer are usually given to three decimal places. Using a full step is a wider and weaker test.
Mark the two test inputs on a number line if the half-step is difficult to see.

blocks.title: Certify another positive root
blocks.prompt: The positive root of \(x^2-7=0\) is required to 2 decimal places. Give the rounded root and the two rounding boundaries, in increasing order.
blocks.hint: Find the place value of the last required digit, then step half that amount in each direction.
blocks.solution:
The rounded value is a candidate. Keep the whole window of inputs that round to the candidate. Its half-width is \(0.005\).

The rounding boundaries are \(2.645\) and \(2.655\). The quadratic is continuous and is increasing on the positive interval.

BoundaryFunction valueSign
\(2.645\)\(-0.003975\)Negative
\(2.655\)\(0.049025\)Positive

The opposite signs locate the root between the two boundaries. Therefore \(2.645<\alpha<2.655\) and \(\alpha\approx2.65\) to 2 decimal places.

sections.title: How do the signs prove the final digits?
sections.label: Test the two rounding boundaries
sections.intro: After finding a candidate, evaluate the original function, once at each boundary. An iteration table alone gives evidence for a guess. If the boundary values have opposite signs and the function is continuous throughout, the sign test locates a root in the correct rounding window.

blocks.html: For a particular root, keep the branch or interval from the question. For example, a positive square root belongs to the positive branch, which is increasing. Show that the interval you use contains the desired root rather than a different solution.
Avoid testing at the candidate twice, or declaring a proof because adjacent displayed iterates happen to agree.
Include enough digits on the two evaluated function values to show their signs clearly.

sections.title: How does the place value change with scale?
sections.label: Use the last significant place
sections.intro: Significant figures start at the first nonzero digit. The same count can mean tenths in one answer and ten-thousandths in a small answer. First identify the position of the last significant digit, then build the corresponding rounding window.

blocks.html: For example, a recorded \(0.0864\) to three significant figures has its last digit in the ten-thousandths place. The two boundaries are \(0.08635\) and \(0.08645\). At a power of ten, look at the neighbouring rounded values on both sides, since their spacing can differ.
Leading zeros affect place value. They do not count as significant digits.
Keep the rounding instruction attached to the answer. A value such as 0.0860 shows three significant figures.

sections.title: What changes when the root is negative?
sections.label: Order the negative endpoints
sections.intro: The lower boundary is always the smaller input and lies to the left on a number line. Around a negative candidate, stepping left means subtracting a positive half-step. The negative branch of a quadratic may have the opposite sign order to the positive branch.

blocks.html: For a continuous crossing, either sign order works. Show the actual signs at the ordered endpoints, and confirm that this is the negative root when the equation also has a positive root.
Do not swap the endpoints when one decimal has a larger absolute value. Negative numbers with larger absolute values lie farther left.
Write the candidate first, then write the lower and upper boundary on separate lines before evaluating.

sections.title: What precision is the question actually asking for?

blocks.html: Keep the precision used for calculation separate from the precision used for the final statement. In a written answer, show any trailing zeros required by the question. Record the sign test with enough digits for the method to be readable even if the final value is shorter.
Do not reuse a shorter displayed result as the next calculator input. This can shift the final rounding.

orig_9709_p3_num_iteration.description: Read fixed-point recurrences, choose valid starting inputs, preserve restrictions and calculate successive approximations at full precision.

sections.title: What do the two subscripts mean?
sections.label: Read the recurrence
sections.intro: An iteration is a sequence of trial values generated by one update rule. The initial value \(x_0\) is supplied or chosen as a starting estimate. The update takes the current trial value as its input and produces the next trial value.

blocks.html: \(x_{n+1}=g(x_n)\) gives \(x_1=g(x_0)\), then \(x_2=g(x_1)\). The subscript records the position in the sequence. The parenthesised expression is the input, not a multiplier.
Putting the initial value into the rule every time simply repeats the first update.
Write a table with an index column. If the start is labelled x1 in the question, use that numbering throughout.

blocks.title: Run a new affine iteration
blocks.prompt: Use \(x_{n+1}=\frac{x_n+11}{4}\) with \(x_0=2\). Calculate \(x_1\), \(x_2\), \(x_3\), each to 4 decimal places.
blocks.hint: Use the preceding output as the next input. Use the stored answer key on your calculator before rounding.
blocks.solution:
Start by entering the initial value and applying the update once. The resulting value, at calculator precision, is the next input.

IndexStarting value for this rowRecorded approximation
\(1\)\(2.0000000\)\(3.2500\)
\(2\)\(3.2500000\)\(3.5625\)
\(3\)\(3.5625000\)\(3.6406\)

The value in the final column is the rounded record of a step. Keep extra digits in the calculator for the next calculation.

If the iterates settle at \(\alpha\), replace the input and output of the update by \(\alpha\). Multiply both sides of the fixed-point equation by the non-zero denominator, then collect the terms in the unknown.

sections.title: Why can the limit solve the original equation?
sections.label: Recover the fixed-point equation
sections.intro: Suppose that nearby terms settle to one value and the update is continuous at that value. Both the inputs and the next outputs then tend to the same number. Substituting it into the update leaves it unchanged.

blocks.html: Write \(\alpha=g(\alpha)\), then reverse the rearrangement to see which original equation is being solved. The intersection of the curve \(y=g(x)\) and the diagonal \(y=x\) displays the same equality.

figure.alt: The line y equals x meets the positive square-root graph between 2 and 3. Its horizontal coordinate is the fixed point.
figure.caption: At the crossing \(x=\sqrt{x+3}\). The same number is both input and output.

blocks.html: Squaring can create a candidate of the wrong sign. A fixed point of a principal square-root rule must be non-negative.
Show the rearrangement from the supplied equation to the stated update. Preserve any conditions along the way.

blocks.title: Reverse a different square-root rearrangement
blocks.prompt: The iteration \(x_{n+1}=\sqrt{x_n+8}\) tends to a value in the domain of the update. Select an equivalent equation for that value and the restriction that belongs with the chosen rearrangement.
blocks.hint: Write the fixed-point equation first, then remove the radical or denominator without losing its domain.
blocks.solution:
At a limit the input and output are the same. Replace both by \(x\) to obtain \(x=\sqrt{x+8}\).

For a fixed point, both sides of the square-root equation are non-negative. Squaring is reversible when this restriction is kept.

Solve \(x^2-x-8=0\) with \(x\ge0\).

sections.title: Which digits do I carry between iterations?
sections.label: Keep full calculator precision
sections.intro: Separate the stored value from the value written in your working. The table communicates a rounded record at each index. Feeding those rounded records back into the calculator changes the process and can make the last few digits unreliable.

blocks.html: Use the calculator’s stored result as the next input. Keep at least two or three extra digits when the question asks to show your approximations, and round the final result only after deciding which approximation to report.
Typing the displayed four-decimal value by hand for the next row can produce different later values.
Use brackets when the preceding value is inside an exponent, a denominator or a radical.

sections.title: Which rearrangement restrictions stay in force?
sections.label: Check permitted inputs
sections.intro: Some updates are defined only for part of the real line. A logarithm needs a positive argument, a real square root needs a non-negative argument, and a denominator must remain nonzero. A starting guess is useful only when the later inputs remain valid.

blocks.html: Separate the domain for evaluating the update from restrictions on the fixed point. For instance, \(g(x)=\sqrt{x+5}\) can be evaluated for \(x\ge-5\), but a solution of \(x=g(x)\) satisfies \(x\ge0\).
Multiplying by a denominator or squaring can change the apparent solution set if you drop the original conditions.
Write any restrictions alongside the transformed equation. Check a candidate against the rule that generated it.

blocks.hint: Write the fixed-point equation first, then remove the radical or denominator without losing its domain.
blocks.solution:
At a limit the input and output are the same. Replace both by \(x\) to obtain \(x=\ln(12-x)\).

Exponentiate both sides and add the unknown. The logarithmic argument must be positive in the original fixed-point equation.

Solve \(\mathrm e^x+x=12\) with \(x<12\).

sections.title: How do I check the answer from the iteration?
sections.label: Substitute into the source equation
sections.intro: The update rule provides a sequence and suggests a candidate root. For an exam question, report the requested terms and explain how a limiting value would satisfy the original equation. Then use a sign-change bracket if the final digits need a separate proof.

blocks.html: For \(x^3+x=c\), isolating the cube term gives \(x=\sqrt[3]{c-x}\). The cube root preserves sign, so the fixed-point equation and the original equation describe the same real solutions. The update can still fail for some equations and starting values.
A short sequence that looks settled is not proof by itself. Check the target formula and the required accuracy.
Trace each row from the stated starting value to show how the requested terms were obtained.

orig_9709_p3_num_convergence.description: Read staircase and cobweb diagrams. Distinguish converging sequences from cycles or diverging updates, and check the accuracy of a numerical root.

sections.title: What do the vertical and horizontal steps do?
sections.label: Read one iteration on a graph
sections.intro: Draw the update and the diagonal on equal scales. On the diagonal the horizontal and vertical coordinates are the same. When you move vertically from the current diagonal point, the horizontal coordinate stays at the current input and the height becomes the next output.

blocks.html: Move horizontally back to the diagonal to use that same height as the next horizontal input. Repeat those two movements, keeping the direction of travel. The horizontal coordinates on the diagonal are the successive terms.

figure.alt: Starting at 0.8, the first two updates give 1.4 and 1.7. Each vertical arrow goes to the update graph and each horizontal arrow returns to y = x. The fixed point is (2, 2).
figure.caption: For \(x_{n+1}=1+\tfrac12x_n\), start at \((x_0,x_0)\) on \(y=x\). Move vertically to the update line, then horizontally back to \(y=x\). The numbers beneath the diagram are the first three inputs.

blocks.html: Moving horizontally first from the initial point swaps the meaning of the input and the output.
Keep the initial value and the first two successive terms labelled when asked for an iteration diagram.

blocks.prompt: Start from \(x_0=2\) and use \(x_{n+1}=4+\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\left(x_n-4\right)\). Give the fixed point and describe what happens to the sides visited and the distances from it.

options.option1: Same side of the fixed point

blocks.hint: Subtract the fixed point from the update, then examine one signed gap at a time.
blocks.solution:
\(x=4+\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)(x-4)\) gives the fixed point \(4\).

Each signed gap is multiplied by \(\frac{1}{2}\). Same side of the fixed point. Distances decrease.

The gap shrinks to zero, so the sequence converges.

sections.title: Can the approximations cross the root and still settle?
sections.label: Read a cobweb diagram
sections.intro: An update can send a value below the fixed point to the other side. If that overshoot becomes smaller each time, the terms can approach the same limit while alternating above and below it. The paths around the intersection are often called a cobweb.

blocks.html: Use the distance as well as the side. In this example the signed gap from two is multiplied by \(-\frac12\). A new sign places the next term on the opposite side, and a smaller magnitude moves it closer.

figure.alt: Starting at 0.8, the first two updates give 2.6 and 1.7. Each vertical arrow goes to the update graph and each horizontal arrow returns to y = x. The fixed point is (2, 2).
figure.caption: For \(x_{n+1}=3-\tfrac12x_n\), start at \((x_0,x_0)\) on \(y=x\). Move vertically to the update line, then horizontally back to \(y=x\). The numbers beneath the diagram are the first three inputs.

blocks.html: Alternation alone does not show failure. It can be part of convergence.

sections.title: What does a sequence moving away look like?
sections.label: Recognise a failed update
sections.intro: Having a fixed point is a fact about the equation. Approaching it from the chosen starting value is a fact about the update. An update can produce terms that move farther from the intersection, so solving the fixed-point equation alone does not predict the calculation.

blocks.html: In a simple linear example you can subtract the fixed point from both sides of the update. Compare the magnitude of the new gap with the old one. This gives a direct explanation for that example, using the recurrence itself.
A valid algebraic rearrangement does not guarantee a useful iteration.
Show the starting value and the first changes when asked to explain why the stated process is unsuitable.
